phase1.intro:
This is the moment everything from lesson one becomes real code instead of just an idea.

Where do you want to start — the blueprint, or the objects built from it?

dialogue: A [[term:class]] is the blueprint — here, `Student`. It declares what every Student will have: [[term:fields]] like `name`, `age`, and `gpa` to hold data, and [[term:methods]] like `displayInfo()` to define behavior.

stickyNote.flavor: 📐 the blueprint, not the thing itself
stickyNote.definition: A class defines the fields (data) and methods (behavior) every object built from it will have. Student is the blueprint here.

topics.buttonText: What's the difference between a class and an object?
dialogue: An [[term:object]] is an actual instance built from that blueprint — `alice` and `bob` are both Students, but with their own separate values sitting in their own fields.
Once alice and bob exist, you reach their fields and methods with dot notation: `alice.name`, `alice.displayInfo()`. Two objects, same blueprint, completely independent data.

stickyNote.flavor: 🏠 the actual house built from the blueprint
stickyNote.definition: An object is an instance of a class, built via new. Each object has its own independent copy of the class's fields.

topics.buttonText: What's the deal with the constructor and this?
dialogue: The [[term:constructor]] is the special method that actually builds a new object: it shares the class's exact name, has no return type at all (not even void), and runs automatically the moment you write `new Student(...)`.

Inside it, you'll almost always see [[term:this]] show up: `this.name = name;` — [[key:this refers to the object currently being built, and it's how Java tells apart the field from the parameter when they share a name]].

stickyNote.flavor: 🔨 the method that builds it, and this points at it
stickyNote.definition: A constructor shares the class name, has no return type, and runs on new ClassName(...). this refers to the current object, disambiguating field vs. parameter.

phase1.openingDialogue: Classes are blueprints, objects are instances built from them — and this is where OOP stops being an idea and starts being code. 🏗️

phase2.explanation:
`void Student(...)` looks almost right, but [[warn:that void is exactly what turns this from a constructor into a regular method]]. A real constructor has NO return type at all — not even void — and it must share the class's name exactly.

Because Java now sees `Student(String, int, double)` as a plain method instead of a constructor, the class is left with no matching constructor at all for `new Student("Alice", 20, 3.8)` to call. [[key:The fix is simply removing void]]: `Student(String name, int age, double gpa) { ... }`, with no return type whatsoever.

phase3.openingDialogue: Time to create your first class! The blueprint of the future~ 🏗️

mcq.question:
Which of these is true about a Java constructor?

A) It must have a return type of void
B) It has the same name as the class and no return type at all
C) It can have any name you want
D) It must always take zero parameters

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create a class called Book with:
• Fields: title (String), author (String), pages (int)
• Constructor that initializes all fields
• Method: displayInfo() that prints all book info

In main, create 2 Book objects and call displayInfo() on both.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: if you don't write ANY constructor at all in a class, Java quietly generates a free no-argument one for you behind the scenes, called the default constructor. The moment you write even one constructor yourself, though, Java stops giving you that free one — which is exactly why some classes seem to lose their plain `new ClassName()` option once you add a custom constructor.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thing before you build your next blueprint~
